text.paragraph: Establishing care with a comprehensive geriatric assessment, after his annual wellness screening elsewhere noted slower walking and a near-fall: gait speed, Timed Up and Go, chair stands, balance, grip strength, MoCA, GDS-15, hearing, vision, nutrition and continence; frailty; a deprescribing review; bone health; what matters most to him; and a geriatric medicine consultation [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants to keep walking into town to teach, and to manage his stairs at home. [S]
Knee pain on stairs and on the hill, and a near-fall on his stairs that frightened him. [S]
He wants no medicine he does not need. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Plato names him in the Protagoras as 'Hippocrates of Cos, the Asclepiad', a physician who took pupils for a fee, and in the Phaedrus cites his method; Aristotle calls him 'the Great Hippocrates'. These are the earliest witnesses to him. [D]

The three ancient lives (by Soranus, a late writer, and in the Suda and Tzetzes, all written many centuries after him) say that he was born on Cos in 460 BC, that his father Heraclides was a physician of the Asclepiad guild and taught him, and that he travelled widely in Greece; the Loeb editor finds 'a certain amount of fable' in them but nothing improbable in their broad outline. [D]

The Hippocratic Corpus is not the work of one man. The Loeb editor describes it as the remains of a library of works 'of various dates and of different schools', a great part of which is 'neither by Hippocrates himself nor by his school'; Aristotle ascribed one of its treatises to Polybus, and Hippocrates is 'a name without writings'. Which treatises, if any, he wrote is still debated. [D]

Modern medicine regards him as its founder: reviews call him 'the father of modern medicine' and 'the founding father of clinical medicine', for medicine based on observation of clinical signs rather than on religious or magical beliefs. [D]

Nothing about his own health is documented in the sources read: no illness, injury or cause of death is recorded. The roster's 'longevity; natural aging' is a lead only, resting on the disputed traditions of his age. [R]

list.item: Physician and teacher of medicine for some seventy years; still teaches pupils two mornings a week, examines their case notes and writes; walks into town for his teaching [S]
Lives alone in his own house in the town, with stairs to the bedroom; a neighbor looks in each day; pupils and friends visit often [S]
Never smoked; one small cup of wine mixed with water at dinner most days (AUDIT-C 1); no other substances [S]
Eats a plain diet of barley, beans, vegetables, fish, cheese and olive oil; drinks water through the day; walks about 2 km a day, less since the knee pain worsened [S]
Strengths: lifelong habits of observation and moderation, a sharp mind, purpose in teaching, friends and pupils around him, and his own wish to stay independent [S]

One to two tablets by mouth every eight hours as needed; no more than six tablets a day

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, courteous and precise; speech fluent; mood good; affect full; no psychotic symptoms; MoCA 26 of 30 (lost points on delayed recall); GDS-15 2. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in all activities of daily living and in instrumental activities (shopping, cooking, his own medicines and money); climbs his stairs with the rail and one foot at a time; walks more slowly and stops to rest on the hill into town; Clinical Frailty Scale 3 (managing well); FRAIL scale 1 of 5 (difficulty climbing stairs), pre-frail. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-03-02; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert, courteous and precise; speech fluent; mood good; affect full; no psychotic symptoms; MoCA 26 of 30 (lost points on delayed recall); GDS-15 2. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Potentially inappropriate over-the-counter medicines (Beers 2023): naproxen most days for about two years and diphenhydramine for sleep three or four nights a week; both stopped at intake: active, confirmed [S]

Comprehensive geriatric assessment at intake: gait speed, Timed Up and Go, 30-second chair stand, four-stage balance test, grip strength, orthostatic blood pressure, MoCA, GDS-15, hearing (whisper test), vision, nutrition (MNA-SF), continence, the Clinical Frailty Scale and the FRAIL scale; what matters most to him (4Ms). Guideline: Age-Friendly Health Systems: the 4Ms (What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility) (2026); Updating STEADI for Primary Care: Recommendations From the American Geriatrics Society Workgroup (2025); Physical Frailty: ICFSR International Clinical Practice Guidelines for Identification and Management (2019) [S]

Geriatric medicine consultation for slower gait and a near-fall in a man of 89: the cause, frailty, the deprescribing plan, falls prevention, bone health and a plan built on what matters most to him. Guideline: Age-Friendly Health Systems: the 4Ms (What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility) (2026); Updating STEADI for Primary Care: Recommendations From the American Geriatrics Society Workgroup (2025); World guidelines for falls prevention and management for older adults: a global initiative (2022) [S]

Deprescribing (Beers 2023): stop over-the-counter naproxen (chronic NSAID use at 89) and diphenhydramine (strongly anticholinergic); acetaminophen up to 3,000 mg a day as needed; sleep routine without a sleep aid; check every over-the-counter purchase with the clinic or pharmacist. Guideline: American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults (2023) [S]

Bone health: 25-hydroxyvitamin D at intake and after repletion; vitamin D3 1,000 units daily; calcium from food (about 1,200 mg a day); DXA of the spine and hips with FRAX. Guideline: The clinician's guide to prevention and treatment of osteoporosis (2022); Osteoporosis in men: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (2012); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]
